body:
# On Niflheimr: a letter to a colleague

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Niflheimr, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely the marks are a nicety. Permit me to use Niflheimr to show they are not.

First, the attestation. The attested form is **ᚾᛁᚠᛚᚼᛁᛘᚱ**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Niflheimr**.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: nIVL-haym-r — the f is soft, sounding as v; the second element glides like 'aim' with an h in front; end with a light trilled r that carries its own syllable. The marks are what carry that sound to a reader who has never heard it spoken.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *niflheimr* differs from the canonical *Niflheimr* only by convention of display — case, not content. It is *acceptable everywhere*: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. Niflheimr needs no borrowing to be explained: its first element is one of the most securely inherited words in the Germanic vocabulary, the same mist that Greek keeps in nephélē, Latin in nebula, and Sanskrit in nábhas — three daughter languages and the North all descended from the same cloud.  The genuine scholarly argument is internal.

And it never stopped working. The mist-world's afterlife runs through every retelling that needs a bottom floor for the cosmos.  Wagner rebuilt it as Nibelheim, the smoke-filled subterranean forge-realm of Alberich in Das Rheingold — a conflation of Niflheimr with the Nibelung dwarf-lore that no saga ever made, and one of the most consequential mistranslations in myth reception.

## The Convention's Own History

The Poetic Edda survives essentially in one manuscript — the Codex Regius, c. 1270 — and normalized Old Norse spelling descends from what that manuscript and its siblings actually write. Þ and ð are not decorations: they are letters of the alphabet the skalds used (and English later abandoned), and ǫ is a nasal vowel the normalization preserves because the sources carry it. The register's rule is the manuscript's rule: spell the names the way the tradition that sang them wrote them down.

## Where Protocol Meets Practice

The technical answer is simple: the canonical marks are legal IDNA 2008 characters, encoded as punycode under `xn--`. The practical answer is messier: legal does not mean stocked (registrar inventory is partial), and stocked does not mean typeable (stacked diacritics defeat mobile keyboards).

So the register's rule is a hierarchy of attested forms — full restoration, circumflex, macron-only, attested variant, and finally plain ASCII for the systems that cannot carry marks. Every rung is defensible because every rung is attested. The forms this register rules against are not rungs; they are errors, and errors do not get rungs.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Niflheimr** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *niflheimr* shares that standing — the two are the same name in every system. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Niflheimr** stands at [/niflheimr/](/niflheimr/).

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 6 cited sources — Poetic Edda: Vafþrúðnismál 20–21 (the Élivágar and the venom-drops that grew into Ymir), 31 (Aurgelmir), 43 (nine worlds below Niflhel); Grímnismál 26 (Eikþyrnir dripping into Hvergelmir, whence all waters flow), 27–29 (the river lists), 34–35 (the serpents under Yggdrasill, Níðhöggr); Baldrs draumar 2 (Óðinn's ride down to Niflhel), Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 3 (evil men go to Hel, thence to Niflhel in the ninth world), 4 (Niflheimr made before the earth; Hvergelmir; the eleven rivers), 5–8 (Muspellsheimr; the rime and the quickening of Ymir), 15–16 (the third root over Niflheimr, Hvergelmir beneath, Níðhöggr gnawing), Cleasby–Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, s.v. nifl-heimr, nifl-hel, heimr, hver-gelmir, él.
